title: Weight Classes, Rulesets & Safety Regulations
scope_note: Covers the full combat-robotics weight class ladder (fairyweight through heavyweight), the major rulesets that govern competitions (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots, AWS/UK, European/Australian variants), weight bonuses for walkers and multibots, banned weapons and materials, safety and inspection requirements, and match/judging rules. Every judgement is biased toward 1 lb antweight and plastic antweight, the classes most builders start in.

entities.name: Fairyweight (150g)
entities.summary: The smallest weight class in common use, capped at 150 grams (about 0.33 lb). In the US/SPARC world it is called Fairyweight; confusingly, this exact 150g limit is what British builders call 'Antweight', which is far lighter than the US 1lb antweight. It is a popular entry point because parts are cheap and damage is minimal.
entities.typical_arena: Small tabletop or club-scale arena (roughly 4-8 ft across), often polycarbonate-walled, shared with antweight-class fights
entities.notes: Robots must also fit within a 150mm x 150mm footprint under UK/AWS rules, with no overhang at any height. Non-rotary/non-rolling locomotion (walkers, shufflers) gets a bonus up to 225g under UK rules (see plastic-antweight and walker-bonus term entries).

entities.name: Antweight (1 lb)
entities.summary: The classic North American entry class, capped at 1 lb (454 g). It is the most-run class at US and Canadian events (SPARC, RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast) and is roughly three times heavier than the UK 'Antweight' (150 g), a naming collision that trips up new builders reading rules from the wrong region.
entities.typical_arena: Small combat box, roughly 8x8 ft to 12x12 ft, polycarbonate walls, often shared with beetleweight
entities.notes: Because it is 3x the mass of the UK fairyweight/antweight, US 1lb antweights typically run larger motors, bigger batteries, and heavier armor than their UK 150g counterparts even though both are called 'antweight'.

entities.name: Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A 1 lb (454 g) variant of antweight in which the entire robot (except electronics, motors, and fasteners) must be built from approved 3D-printable/thermoplastic materials. Started by Western Allied Robotics to make antweight building cheaper and more accessible, later folded into SPARC as an official weight-class variant. It is the fastest-growing beginner class because a full robot can be printed on a hobby FDM printer for well under $50.
entities.typical_arena: Same box as regular antweight; often run in mixed brackets with antweight
entities.notes: Allowed materials under SPARC: PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, and PET. Banned: TPU, nylon, and any fiber-filled/composite plastic (carbon-fiber or fiberglass-loaded filament), and any metal structural part beyond fasteners, motors, bearings, and electronics. This keeps damage rates and repair costs very low, which is exactly why it is recommended as the first build for new competitors.

entities.name: Beetleweight (3 lb)
entities.summary: A 3 lb (1.36 kg) class, the second most popular class in the US after antweight, and one of NHRL's three official divisions. It allows meaningfully more powerful weapons and drivetrains than antweight while still being affordable and easy to transport.
entities.typical_arena: Mid-size combat box, roughly 12x12 ft to 24x24 ft polycarbonate arena

entities.name: Plastic Beetleweight
entities.summary: The 3 lb equivalent of plastic antweight: robots must be built almost entirely from approved 3D-printable plastics rather than metal. Less common than plastic antweight but growing at the same regional US events that run plastic-only brackets.
entities.notes: Uses the same allowed-material list as plastic antweight (PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, PET; no TPU, nylon, or fiber-filled composites).

entities.name: Hobbyweight (12 lb)
entities.summary: A 12 lb (5.44 kg) middle-tier class, one of NHRL's three flagship divisions and a common SPARC class. It's a step up in cost and danger from beetleweight, generally viewed as an intermediate builder's class.

entities.name: Featherweight (30 lb)
entities.summary: A 30 lb (13.6 kg) class, NHRL's largest flagship division and a long-standing SPARC/RoboGames class. Featherweight fights are visibly more destructive than smaller classes and require more serious safety gear and containment.

entities.name: Lightweight (60 lb)
entities.summary: A 60 lb (27.2 kg) class run mainly by SPARC and RoboGames. It sits between the popular small hobby classes and the TV-scale heavyweights, requiring real machine-shop fabrication and industrial-grade components.

entities.name: Middleweight (120 lb)
entities.summary: A 120 lb (54.4 kg) class run by SPARC and RoboGames, sitting just below the TV-scale heavyweight class. Robots at this size need hydraulic/pneumatic or large brushless weapon systems and significant safety infrastructure.

entities.name: Heavyweight (220-250 lb)
entities.summary: The top-tier 'TV weight' class. BattleBots' modern single division caps at 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, while SPARC's traditional heavyweight class is 220 lb (100 kg); RoboGames also runs a 250 lb class plus a heavier walking-bonus tier. These robots require professional-grade fabrication, hydraulics/large brushless weapons, and are only run at events with heavy-duty arenas.
entities.typical_arena: Reinforced steel/polycarbonate arena (e.g. BattleBox), often with hazards (pulverizer, screws)
entities.notes: Exact heavyweight cap differs by organization: BattleBots = 250 lb (500 lb if a qualifying walker), classic SPARC heavyweight = 220 lb, RoboGames runs both a 250 lb class and a 500 lb walking-bonus tier. Always check the specific event's rulebook rather than assuming one universal 'heavyweight' number.

entities.name: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
entities.summary: SPARC is the dominant unified US/international rule set for hobby-scale combat robotics. A single 'SPARC-legal' build is accepted at essentially every SPARC-compliant event worldwide, covering weight classes from fairyweight (150g) up to heavyweight (220 lb), plastic-class material rules, weight bonuses for walkers/shufflers, multibot/clusterbot rules, and standardized safety requirements.
entities.organization: SPARC (community-maintained standard, not a single company)
entities.version: maintained on a rolling basis at sparc.tools (this research references the v1.2-derived rules and later community revisions)
key_rules: Weight classes: Fairyweight 150g, Antweight 1lb, Beetleweight 3lb, Mantisweight 6lb, Hobbyweight 12lb, Dogeweight 15lb, Featherweight 30lb, Lightweight 60lb, Middleweight 120lb, Heavyweight 220lb
Walkers (no rolling/cam-based ground contact) get a 100% weight bonus (double normal class weight)
Shufflers/non-wheeled-but-not-full-walkers may get up to a 50% weight bonus depending on locomotion type
Plastic-class variants (Plastic Antweight, Plastic Beetleweight) restrict construction to approved 3D-printable plastics only
Multibot/clusterbot teams share the class weight limit, with extra allowance if all members are walkers

entities.name: NHRL Open Rules (National Havoc Robot League)
entities.summary: NHRL runs the largest recurring US combat robotics series (Franklin, MA) across exactly three weight classes: 3lb (beetleweight), 12lb (hobbyweight), and 30lb (featherweight). It uses a qualifying-then-bracket tournament format, mandatory weapon locks and radio failsafe testing, and pays cash prizes, which distinguishes it from most hobbyist-only events.
key_rules: Three weight classes only: 3lb, 12lb, 30lb, weighed at or below the max at the start of each fight
Non-Traditional Locomotion bonus: +1.5lb (3lb class), +6lb (12lb class), +15lb (30lb class) — a 50% bonus
True Walker bonus: +3lb (3lb class), +12lb (12lb class), +30lb (30lb class) — a 100% bonus, doubling the class weight
Every robot needs a weapon lock preventing spinning weapons from moving outside the cage, and a tool-free external power-off
All robots must pass a radio failsafe test before competing
3-minute matches; win by tap-out, knockout, or judges' decision if time expires
Two-stage tournament: Qualifying rounds then a single-elimination Bracket; top 50% by NHRL ranking are seeded
banned: entanglement devices, defined as any component designed to entangle in the rotational or moving parts of the opponent
liquids expelled from the bot, except liquid used purely as a fuel source or liquid that becomes gaseous shortly after leaving the bot / before hitting the opponent
tethered projectiles designed in a way likely to entangle the opponent
domain knowledge: general SPARC-aligned bans on explosives and EMP/RF-jamming also apply

entities.name: RoboGames Combat Robot Rules
entities.summary: RoboGames (formerly ROBOlympics) is a large annual US multi-discipline robotics expo whose combat division runs six standard weight classes (150g through 250lb) plus parallel walking-bonus classes at 100% extra weight and separate 1lb/3lb autonomous divisions. It has one of the most detailed public banned-weapon and judging-scoring rulesets of any hobby organization.
key_rules: Regular classes: 150g, 1lb, 3lb, 60lb, 120lb, 250lb
Walking-bonus classes (100% weight bonus over regular class): 300g, 2lb, 6lb, 120lb, 240lb, 500lb
Separate 1lb and 3lb autonomous-robot divisions
Manual main power disconnect must be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator; full deactivation within 60 seconds
Weapon lock must be a clearly visible, high-visibility (neon orange or similar) physical locking device, in place during power-on
Radio must use digitally coded, mated transmitter/receiver pairs with a fail-safe; toy-grade and AM-band systems are banned
Judging: 3-judge panel, each judge scores Aggression (max 5 points) and Damage (max 6 points) = 11 points per judge, 33 total
Pinning capped at 15 seconds before the pinned robot must be released
banned: heat weapons except specially approved flamethrowers

entities.name: BattleBots Design & Safety Rules
entities.summary: BattleBots is the flagship US televised combat robotics league, running one professional heavyweight division at 250 lb ready-to-fight (up to 500 lb for a qualifying articulated-leg walker). Lifting/flipping weapons must pass a functional test lifting 250 lb to 12 inches before being allowed to compete, and every robot goes through a rigorous in-person tech and safety inspection ('the box') before being cleared to fight.
entities.version: Design Rules Rev. 2020.0 baseline (later seasons carry incremental updates)
key_rules: Single standard weight class: 250.0 lb maximum ready-to-fight
Walking-bonus allowance: up to 500.0 lb if the robot walks via articulated legs and meets additional design criteria
Any lifting or grappling weapon must demonstrate it can lift 250 lb to a height of 12 inches during inspection
Full in-person technical/safety inspection ('the box') required before every event
3-judge panel scores on an 11-point scale when a match goes the distance without a KO: 5 points for Damage, 3 points for Aggression, 3 points for Control (recent-season point split)
Damage is scored on relative non-cosmetic damage dealt, including systems that stop working correctly by match end, and can include self-inflicted damage
Aggression is scored on frequency, severity, boldness, and intent of attacks the robot deliberately initiates
Control is scored on how well and how long a robot controls the fight: pushing, lifting, pinning the opponent, or using the arena against them
Ahead of the BattleBots Pro League (2026), the judging system was revised to combine Aggression with 'Engagement' into a single 5-point scored category
banned: domain knowledge: standard combat-robotics banned list applies (entanglement, liquids, uncontained fire without approval, explosives, EMP/jamming, unlicensed high-power lasers)
entities.notes: Judging point split (5 Damage / 3 Aggression / 3 Control on an 11-point scale) reflects the Judges' Guide used in recent seasons (Rev. 2021.0/2022.0); BattleBots has revised its judging system across seasons (e.g. the 2026 Pro League merges Aggression and Engagement), so builders/analysts should check the current-season Judges' Guide PDF rather than assume this split is permanent.

entities.name: Antweight World Series Rules (UK)
entities.summary: The Antweight World Series (AWS) is the primary UK/European antweight ruleset, run in association with Bristol Bot Builders. It defines UK-scale classes far lighter than their US namesakes (Antweight 150g roller / 225g non-roller, Fleaweight 75g/113g, Nanoweight 25g/38g), a detailed banned-weapons list, and specific electrical/radio/battery safety rules distinct from US SPARC practice.
entities.organization: Antweight World Series / Bristol Bot Builders
key_rules: Antweight: 150g for rollers, 225g for non-rollers (50% non-roller bonus)
Fleaweight: 75g roller / 113g non-roller
Nanoweight: 25g roller / 38g non-roller
Clusterbot roller allowance formula: Roller weight = Roller Limit - (2/3 x Total non-roller weight)
Allowed radio frequencies: 27MHz, 40MHz, 418MHz, 433-434MHz, 868MHz, and 2.45GHz
Battery max 24V, and batteries must not contain liquid acid or free electrolyte
Weapons must be remotely deactivable; pressurized systems capped at 100 psi (7 bar); detachable weapon parts must be tethered (max 3 ft / 914mm)
Matches run 3 minutes max; 10-second immobility countdown ends a fight; pinning capped at 20 seconds; touching the pit floor is an automatic loss

entities.name: Fighting Robots Association (FRA) Build Rules
entities.summary: The Fighting Robots Association publishes build rules used across a number of UK and continental European combat events, complementing the AWS antweight-specific ruleset with guidance that spans a wider range of weight classes and general safety practice for European events.
key_rules: General European build/safety rules referenced by multiple UK/EU events
Complements AWS for weight classes above antweight
entities.notes: Full rule text was found only as a PDF (2024 FRA build rules) via a French mirror (makerfight.fr); detailed clauses were not individually verified in this pass — treat specifics as low confidence pending a direct read of the PDF.

entities.name: RoboWars Australia Weight Classes & Rules
entities.summary: The Australian combat robotics scene (RoboWars Australia) follows essentially the same SPARC-style weight ladder used in the US and Canada, not the lighter UK/AWS scale: Antweight is 1 lb (454 g), matching US antweight rather than the UK's 150 g class. Australia's ladder additionally runs a Super Heavyweight class at 340 lb (154 kg), one tier above the common 220 lb heavyweight, plus a separate off-arena 'UltiBot' outdoor-terrain division.
key_rules: Weight ladder: Antweight 1lb/454g, Beetleweight 3lb/1.36kg, Mantisweight 6lb/2.72kg, Hobbyweight 12lb/5.44kg, Featherweight 30lb/13.6kg, Lightweight 60lb/27.21kg, Middleweight 120lb/54.43kg, Heavyweight 220lb/99.79kg, Super Heavyweight 340lb/154.22kg
100% weight bonus for non-wheeled (walking) robots at most weight classes
Reduced 35% non-wheeled weight bonus specifically at the 340lb Super Heavyweight tier
Separate 'UltiBot' division for outdoor-terrain combat robots: 30kg for a mobile entrant, 25kg for a fixed/stationary entrant
Rules framework is explicitly based on the SPARC ruleset rather than a wholly separate Australian standard
banned: domain knowledge: follows standard SPARC-aligned banned weapon list (entanglement, liquids, explosives, EMP/jamming, uncontained flame)
entities.notes: This corrects an earlier, less reliable search snippet that had conflated Australian antweight with the UK's 150g standard; a direct read of the RoboWars Australia wiki confirms Australia actually uses the heavier 1lb/454g US-style antweight class.

entities.name: RoboGames
entities.summary: The largest general-purpose robotics competition and expo in the US, featuring a large combat robotics division alongside other robot sports. Combat weight classes run from 150g fairyweight through 250lb heavyweight, plus walking-bonus and autonomous divisions.
entities.location: San Mateo/San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA (historic venue; has moved between events)

entities.name: NHRL (National Havoc Robot League) Events
entities.summary: NHRL's recurring monthly-style live events in the Boston area are the highest-frequency, highest-production-value hobby combat robotics series in the US, running 3lb/12lb/30lb brackets with cash prizes and full livestreaming.
entities.cadence: Multiple events per year (roughly monthly during season)

entities.name: BattleBots (TV Series & Live Events)
entities.summary: The best-known televised combat robotics competition, running a single professional 250lb heavyweight division (up to 500lb for qualifying walkers) with a dedicated fighting arena (the BattleBox) and celebrity/expert judging panels.
entities.location: Various US studio/arena venues (historically Long Beach and Las Vegas)

entities.name: Motorama
entities.summary: One of the longest-running US combat robotics events, historically held in Pennsylvania and now associated with Doswell, Virginia. Runs SPARC-aligned weight classes with a strong antweight/beetleweight/plastic-antweight community presence, and is a well-known season-opener on the US hobby calendar.
entities.notes: Exact current-year class list and venue should be confirmed against the event's own page each season; this entry reflects general/historical pattern rather than a single verified current-year program.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus
entities.summary: A US SPARC-compliant combat robotics event run in conjunction with Maker Faire Orlando, popular with antweight and plastic-antweight builders. Insect weight classes (fairyweight/antweight/beetleweight) run double-elimination, while the larger 12lb/30lb/30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss fight format instead.
entities.location: Central Florida Fairgrounds, 4603 W Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL, USA (co-located with Maker Faire Orlando)

entities.name: Bot Blast
entities.summary: An annual US insectweight-focused combat robotics event running a modified SPARC ruleset. Its main deviations from stock SPARC are a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots, an immediate KO (at official discretion) for any robot with an exposed/damaged LiPo battery, and simplified judging criteria versus full SPARC judging.
entities.notes: The exposed-LiPo-equals-immediate-KO rule is a notable Bot-Blast-specific safety escalation beyond baseline SPARC, directly reflecting how seriously LiPo fire risk is treated in the hobby.

entities.name: Antweight World Series Championship (UK)
entities.summary: The championship event of the UK Antweight World Series circuit, the top competitive target for UK-scale 150g antweight, fleaweight, and nanoweight builders, run under the AWS ruleset via Bristol Bot Builders.
entities.organization: Antweight World Series / Bristol Bot Builders
entities.cadence: Annual championship, feeding from a season of qualifying events

entities.name: Walker/Non-Wheeled Weight Bonus
entities.summary: A weight allowance given to robots that move without continuous rolling or cam-driven contact with the floor, since true walking mechanisms are heavier and less efficient than wheels for a given weight. Typical bonus is +100% (double weight) for a full walker and roughly +50% for shufflers/other non-wheeled-but-not-strict-walker locomotion.
entities.notes: SPARC: 100% bonus for true walkers, up to 50% for shufflers. NHRL: True Walker = +100% (e.g. 3lb class robot may weigh 6lb); Non-Traditional Locomotion = +50% (e.g. 3lb class robot may weigh 4.5lb). RoboGames: walking-bonus classes are exactly double the regular class weight (150g->300g, 1lb->2lb, 3lb->6lb, 120lb->240lb, 250lb->500lb). AWS (UK): non-roller antweight bonus is 50% (150g->225g).

entities.name: Multibot / Clusterbot
entities.summary: A single competition entry made of two or more physically separate robots controlled together as one 'weapon system,' sharing the weight limit of their class. Rules typically require all sub-units to be destroyed/immobilized for the team to lose, and extra weight allowance can apply if all sub-units are walkers.
entities.notes: Example from SPARC-style rules: a 12lb class multibot made of one walker/one shuffler is allowed 18lb total; a 12lb multibot made of two full walkers is allowed 24lb total. AWS (UK) clusterbots mixing roller and non-roller units use the formula: Roller allowance = Roller class limit - (2/3 x total non-roller weight), which prevents teams from gaming the non-roller bonus by loading most of the mass into non-rolling parts.

entities.name: Tap-Out
entities.summary: A rule allowing a robot's driver to voluntarily concede a match (usually by a verbal call or a pit-crew signal to the referee) to stop the fight before further damage or danger occurs. Common across NHRL, SPARC-style events, and AWS.

entities.name: Knockout (KO) / Immobility Count
entities.summary: A robot that shows no controlled, purposeful movement for a set count (commonly 10 seconds) is ruled 'out' and the match ends in the opponent's favor, similar to a boxing knockout. AWS/UK rules use a 10-second countdown; many US events use similar counts, sometimes referee-judged rather than a strict clock.

entities.name: Pit / Arena Hazard
entities.summary: A hole, drop, or automated hazard (spikes, hammers, saws) built into some arenas that can end a match instantly if a robot falls in or is forced into it — commonly touching the bottom of a pit is an automatic loss under UK/AWS-style rules. Larger UK 'house robot'-style arenas historically had multiple hazards; most hobby-class US arenas are simpler flat boxes without hazards.

entities.name: Weapon Lock
entities.summary: A required, highly visible physical device (often neon orange) that mechanically prevents a weapon (spinner, lifter, hammer) from moving while the robot is powered but outside the arena — during pit setup, transport, and pre-match staging. Inspectors check that it is fitted before power-on and removed only once the robot is placed in the arena.

entities.name: Radio Fail-Safe
entities.summary: A required behavior of the receiver/ESC system: if the transmitter signal is lost (turned off, out of range, or interfered with), all motion (drive and weapon) must stop automatically rather than continue at the last commanded value. Nearly universal requirement (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, AWS) and is actively tested by inspectors turning off the transmitter during check-in.

entities.name: Removable Link / Master Power Switch
entities.summary: A tool-free, externally accessible way to fully disconnect the main battery from the rest of the robot. Many rulesets require both a switch (for routine on/off) and, for larger classes, a physically removable link/jumper as a secondary, more certain isolation method that a marshal or the builder can pull in an emergency without needing the switch to still be functional.
entities.notes: RoboGames requires the disconnect to be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator, with full deactivation achievable within 60 seconds. AWS requires it be operable without tools. This is one of the first things a tech inspector checks.

entities.name: Plastic-Class Material Restriction
entities.summary: The defining rule of plastic antweight/plastic beetleweight: the entire structure must be built from an approved list of 3D-printable/injection-moldable plastics, excluding electronics, motors, fasteners, and bearings. This keeps cost and damage low, which is why plastic antweight is recommended as a first build.
entities.notes: Approved under SPARC: PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, PET. Banned: TPU, nylon, and any fiber-reinforced/composite filament (carbon-fiber or fiberglass loaded).

entities.name: Pinning Time Limit
entities.summary: A rule capping how long one robot may hold or corner an opponent without active combat, to prevent stalling wins. Typical limits: 15-20 seconds before the referee orders separation or the pin counts against the pinning robot; cornering an opponent against the wall is generally treated the same as a physical pin.

entities.name: Tethered Detachable Weapon Rule
entities.summary: A safety rule requiring that any weapon part designed to detach in combat (e.g. a thrown hammer head or a shattering disc meant to break away) remain physically tethered to the main robot body, with a maximum tether length, to prevent uncontrolled projectiles reaching the crowd or arena walls.
entities.notes: AWS (UK) caps detachable-weapon tethers at 3 feet (914mm) and caps pressurized weapon systems at 100 psi (7 bar).

entities.name: Judges' Decision
entities.summary: When a match runs its full time without a knockout or tap-out, a panel of judges (commonly 3) decides the winner using weighted criteria, most often a mix of damage dealt, aggression/control shown, and (in some rulesets) strategy. RoboGames formalizes this as Aggression (max 5 pts) + Damage (max 6 pts) per judge, for 33 total points across a 3-judge panel.
entities.notes: Damage severity is often bucketed (e.g. trivial/cosmetic/minor/significant/major/massive) rather than scored as a raw number, then translated into judge points. Exact weighting varies significantly by organization; BattleBots' precise public point breakdown was not confirmed in this research pass (confidence: low for BattleBots specifically).

entities.name: LiPo Battery Safety Handling
entities.summary: A set of near-universal pit-safety practices for lithium-polymer batteries used in combat robots: charge only in a fireproof LiPo bag or vented metal/ammo box, never leave a charging battery unattended, inspect for swelling/puncture damage before every use, and store/transport in fire-resistant bags. Several major events (e.g. RoboGames 2017) have had LiPo fires in the pits, which is why fireproof bags are now commonly mandatory rather than optional.
entities.notes: Arenas/venues are commonly required to be ventilated for roughly one full air exchange every 60 seconds, and pit areas should have a clear evacuation path in case of a battery fire.

chunks.title: The Full Combat Robotics Weight Class Ladder
chunks.body_md:
Combat robotics weight classes form a ladder from a few hundred grams up to a couple hundred pounds, and almost every rule in the sport (armor thickness, weapon energy, safety inspection strictness, arena construction) scales with which rung a robot sits on. From smallest to largest, the classes most builders encounter are:

| Class | Limit (lb) | Limit (kg/g) | Typical orgs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fairyweight | 0.33 lb | 150 g | SPARC, RoboGames |
| Antweight (US) | 1 lb | 454 g | SPARC, RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast |
| Plastic Antweight | 1 lb | 454 g | SPARC and most US regional events |
| Beetleweight | 3 lb | 1.36 kg | SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, Motorama |
| Plastic Beetleweight | 3 lb | 1.36 kg | SPARC and regional US events |
| Hobbyweight | 12 lb | 5.44 kg | NHRL, SPARC |
| Featherweight | 30 lb | 13.6 kg | NHRL, SPARC, RoboGames |
| Lightweight | 60 lb | 27.2 kg | SPARC, RoboGames |
| Middleweight | 120 lb | 54.4 kg | SPARC, RoboGames |
| Heavyweight | 220-250 lb | 100-113 kg | BattleBots (250 lb), SPARC (220 lb), RoboGames (250 lb) |

For a beginner, the practical takeaway is that antweight (1 lb) and its plastic-only sibling, plastic antweight, sit at the bottom of the US ladder for a reason: they are the cheapest and safest classes to build and fight in, they are run at nearly every event on the calendar, and they teach the same design, wiring, and driving skills that scale up to every heavier class later. The UK runs an entirely separate, much lighter ladder starting at 150g 'Antweight' (see the fairyweight/antweight naming-confusion chunk), so a US builder reading a UK rulebook, or vice versa, needs to check units and grams/pounds carefully before assuming a class name means the same thing.

No single number is 'the' heavyweight limit: BattleBots' TV division is 250 lb, RoboGames also runs 250 lb (with a 500 lb walking-bonus tier), and older/traditional SPARC heavyweight rules cap at 220 lb. Always confirm the exact number against the specific event's current rulebook rather than assuming cross-organization consistency, especially at the top of the ladder where the difference between 220 lb and 250 lb is a real, non-trivial design constraint.

chunks.title: Why 'Antweight' Means Two Different Weights (US vs UK)
chunks.body_md:
One of the most common points of confusion for a new builder researching antweight combat robots online is that 'Antweight' does not mean the same weight everywhere. In the United States, and under the SPARC standard used by most North American events (RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast), Antweight is a 1 lb (454 g) class. In the United Kingdom, under the Antweight World Series (AWS) rules run through Bristol Bot Builders, 'Antweight' is only 150 g for a roller-locomotion robot (225 g if it uses non-rolling locomotion) — roughly a third of the US weight.

This 150 g UK number is exactly what US/SPARC terminology calls 'Fairyweight.' So a build video, forum post, or parts list that says 'antweight' could be describing a robot three times heavier than another build also labeled 'antweight,' purely because of which country's rules the author is using. The practical effects run deep: a US 1 lb antweight can carry a meaningfully bigger battery, a heavier drive motor pair, and thicker armor than a UK 150 g antweight, so motor/ESC/battery recommendations, weapon tip speeds, and even typical arena sizes differ between the two 'antweight' scenes even though the robots look similar in silhouette.

When reading any antweight rule, spec sheet, or parts recommendation, the single most important thing to check first is whether the source is using US/SPARC units (1 lb / 454 g class) or UK/AWS units (150 g class, with a separate lighter Fleaweight at 75 g and Nanoweight at 25 g below it). Below UK antweight, AWS runs Fleaweight (75 g roller / 113 g non-roller) and Nanoweight (25 g roller / 38 g non-roller) — classes that have no direct US equivalent at all, since the US ladder jumps straight from a much heavier 1 lb antweight up to 3 lb beetleweight with nothing smaller. A builder targeting an international audience, or ordering parts from a UK antweight supplier for a US 1 lb build, should always convert and double-check the actual gram/pound figure rather than relying on the class name alone.

chunks.title: Plastic Antweight: Rules, Materials, and Why It's the Best First Build
chunks.body_md:
Plastic antweight is a 1 lb (454 g) class variant that restricts the robot's structure to a defined list of 3D-printable/thermoplastic materials, with electronics, motors, fasteners, and bearings exempted from the material restriction. It was started by Western Allied Robotics specifically to lower the cost and skill barrier of entering antweight combat, and the rule has since been folded into the broader SPARC standard so it is recognized at essentially any SPARC-compliant US event.

Under SPARC's plastic-class rules, the approved structural materials are PLA, PLA+, ABS, PETG, ASA, and PET — all common, cheap, easy-to-print filaments available from any hobby 3D printer supplier. Explicitly banned are TPU (too soft/flexible to give a fair strength-per-weight comparison and complicates armor rules), nylon (much tougher and more expensive to print reliably), and any fiber-reinforced or composite filament such as carbon-fiber-loaded or fiberglass-loaded nylon/PETG, which would defeat the purpose of a low-cost, low-performance-ceiling class by letting well-funded builders buy their way to metal-like strength.

The practical effect of this restriction is a class where damage is dramatically lower than a comparable metal antweight: plastic armor cracks, chips, and deforms rather than punching through, plastic weapons tend to shatter rather than embed, and a whole robot can typically be printed and assembled for well under $50 in material cost, with the most expensive parts being the motor, battery, receiver, and ESC — all of which are reusable across many builds even after the printed chassis is destroyed. This is exactly why plastic antweight, alongside 150 g fairyweight, is the class most consistently recommended to first-time combat robot builders: mistakes are cheap, a printer replaces broken parts overnight, and the skills learned (weight budgeting, wiring, driving, basic weapon design) transfer directly to metal antweight and beetleweight later. Because the class shares the same 1 lb weight limit as regular antweight, plastic antweight robots are frequently run in the same event bracket as metal antweights, though many clubs and regional events (Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast, and others) also run a dedicated plastic-only bracket to keep matches fairer between plastic and metal builds.

chunks.title: Weight Bonuses: Walkers, Shufflers, and Multibots Across Organizations
chunks.body_md:
Because a true walking mechanism (linked legs with no continuous rolling or cam contact against the floor) is mechanically heavier and less power-efficient than a wheel for the same ground speed, essentially every major ruleset gives walking robots a weight allowance over the standard class limit, and several give a smaller allowance to 'shufflers' or other non-wheeled-but-not-strictly-walking locomotion.

**SPARC**: true walkers get a 100% bonus (i.e. double the normal class weight), and shufflers or other qualifying non-wheeled locomotion can get up to a 50% bonus, depending on exactly how the mechanism contacts the floor. A walker is formally defined as having no rolling elements and no continuous rolling or cam-operated motion in contact with the floor, directly or through a linkage — a strict definition meant to stop 'fake walkers' (e.g. a wheel disguised inside a leg-shaped shroud) from claiming the bonus.

**NHRL**: publishes exact numbers per class. Non-Traditional Locomotion gives +1.5 lb in the 3 lb class, +6 lb in the 12 lb class, and +15 lb in the 30 lb class (a 50% bonus). True Walker status gives +3 lb, +12 lb, and +30 lb respectively in those same classes — a full 100% bonus, meaning a 3 lb-class true walker may legally weigh 6 lb.

**RoboGames**: runs entirely separate 'walking-bonus classes' that are exactly double the corresponding standard class: 150 g becomes 300 g, 1 lb becomes 2 lb, 3 lb becomes 6 lb, 120 lb becomes 240 lb, and 250 lb becomes 500 lb.

**BattleBots**: heavyweight is normally 250 lb, but a robot that walks via articulated legs and meets additional design criteria may compete up to 500 lb — again a 100% bonus, matching the pattern seen everywhere else.

**AWS (UK)**: antweight is 150 g for roller-locomotion robots but 225 g for non-roller robots, a 50% bonus rather than 100%, reflecting the UK ruleset's generally tighter tolerances at these very small masses.

Multibot/clusterbot teams (two or more separately-armored robots fighting as one entry) share their class's weight limit across all sub-units, with further bonuses if every sub-unit qualifies as a walker. A worked SPARC-style example: a 12 lb class multibot made of one walker and one shuffler gets an 18 lb combined allowance, while a 12 lb multibot made of two full walkers gets 24 lb. AWS handles mixed roller/non-roller clusterbots with an explicit formula: Roller allowance = Roller class limit − (2/3 × total non-roller weight), which prevents a team from gaming the system by putting almost all of the robot's mass into non-rolling parts to harvest the bonus.

chunks.title: SPARC: The Unified US Combat Robotics Standard
chunks.body_md:
SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat) exists to solve a coordination problem: before it, every regional US combat robotics event wrote its own rulebook, and a robot legal at one event could be illegal at the next over some tiny weight or safety difference. SPARC is a community-maintained rules standard (hosted at sparc.tools) that most active US antweight/beetleweight/hobbyweight-and-up events now adopt wholesale or with only minor local additions, so a 'SPARC-legal' robot travels between events without a rebuild.

SPARC's weight ladder runs Fairyweight (150 g), Antweight (1 lb), Beetleweight (3 lb), Mantisweight (6 lb), Hobbyweight (12 lb), Dogeweight (15 lb), Featherweight (30 lb), Lightweight (60 lb), Middleweight (120 lb), and Heavyweight (220 lb), each with its own safety and construction requirements scaled to the destructive potential of that class. On top of the base ladder, SPARC layers several important variant rules: the plastic-class rules (Plastic Antweight, Plastic Beetleweight) restricting construction to a defined list of 3D-printable plastics; the walker/shuffler weight-bonus rules (100% for true walkers, up to 50% for shufflers); and multibot/clusterbot rules governing how weight is shared and bonused across multiple physically separate robots fighting as one entry.

Safety-wise, SPARC-aligned events converge on the same core requirements found across nearly every other ruleset in this space: a tool-free external main power disconnect, a radio system with a fail-safe that halts all motion on signal loss, a visible weapon lock fitted whenever the robot is powered outside the arena, and a banned-weapons list excluding entanglement devices, liquid/fluid weapons, unlicensed flame weapons, explosives, and RF-jamming/EMP weapons. Because SPARC is community-maintained rather than owned by a single company, exact wording and edge-case rulings can evolve between events and years, so competitors are expected to check the current version at sparc.tools rather than relying on an older cached copy — a real risk when researching the rules from an old PDF or forum thread, since the version referenced by many public sources is the older v1.2 document rather than the latest text.

chunks.title: NHRL: Cash-Prize Tournament Rules for 3/12/30 lb Classes
chunks.body_md:
The National Havoc Robot League (NHRL) runs the highest-frequency, highest-production hobby combat robotics series in the US, based in Franklin, Massachusetts, and is notable for being one of the few organizations to pay real cash prizes to winners and runners-up rather than running purely for trophies/bragging rights. NHRL deliberately keeps its class list narrow — exactly three weight classes: 3 lb (branded internally alongside 'beetleweight'), 12 lb ('hobbyweight'), and 30 lb ('featherweight') — which lets it build a deep, well-refined ruleset and arena for each class rather than spreading effort across a dozen weight tiers.

Each class carries two distinct weight bonuses. 'Non-Traditional Locomotion' (any drive that isn't simple wheels, but doesn't rise to the strict walker definition) is worth a 50% weight bonus: +1.5 lb in the 3 lb class, +6 lb in the 12 lb class, +15 lb in the 30 lb class. 'True Walker' status is worth a full 100% bonus, doubling the class weight outright: +3 lb, +12 lb, and +30 lb respectively. This two-tier bonus structure mirrors what most other US rulesets do, just documented with unusually explicit numbers.

Safety and inspection requirements are strict and specifically tested at check-in: every robot must carry a weapon lock that physically prevents any spinning weapon from moving outside the arena cage, must have a way to fully power down without disassembly (a switch or removable link operable without tools), and must pass an active radio fail-safe test where an inspector or the driver deliberately kills the transmitter to confirm the robot goes fully inert.

Matches run 3 minutes. NHRL's tournament format is genuinely two-stage rather than a single bracket: a Qualifying stage first, where a robot needs two wins across up to three preliminary rounds (Opening/Round 1, then either The Cusp or Redemption/Round 2, and potentially a decisive Bubble/Round 3) to advance into the actual single-elimination Bracket stage. The top 50% of entrants, ranked by NHRL's ongoing ranking system, are seeded directly rather than starting from the bottom of the qualifying ladder — rewarding consistent past performance across the league's many events per year. A match itself ends by tap-out, knockout (extended controlled immobility), or, if the full 3 minutes elapses with both robots still mobile, a judges' decision.

chunks.title: RoboGames: Detailed Banned-Weapons List and Point-Scored Judging
chunks.body_md:
RoboGames (originally launched as ROBOlympics) is one of the largest general robotics expos in the US, and its combat robotics division is notable for publishing one of the most granular and explicit rulesets in the hobby — both in terms of banned weapons and in terms of exactly how judges score an undecided fight.

RoboGames runs six standard weight classes: 150 g, 1 lb, 3 lb, 60 lb, 120 lb, and 250 lb, plus a full parallel set of walking-bonus classes at exactly double each of those weights (300 g, 2 lb, 6 lb, 120 lb, 240 lb, and 500 lb), and separate 1 lb and 3 lb autonomous-robot divisions for robots that fight without a human driver in the loop.

The banned list is unusually specific, organized loosely around 'invisible damage' weapons (things that hurt a robot's electronics or control system without visible physical damage, which judges and audiences can't easily verify) and 'arena-damaging' weapons (things that would contaminate or damage the fighting surface for the next match): banned items include electrical/RF-jamming weapons, EMF/magnetic fields aimed at disrupting an opponent's electronics, entanglement devices (nets, tape, string), liquid weapons and any weapon that spills liquid, powders, sand, or ball bearings, foams and liquefied gases, untethered projectiles, heat/flame weapons except specially pre-approved flamethrowers, explosives and flammable solids, blinding lights and smoke, and internal combustion engines.

Safety requirements include a manual main power disconnect operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator and full deactivation achievable within 60 seconds, a weapon lock that must be a clearly visible high-visibility color (neon orange or similar) fitted whenever the robot is powered outside the arena, and a radio system requirement for digitally coded, mated transmitter/receiver pairs with fail-safe — explicitly banning toy-grade radio systems and anything on the AM band.

When a match goes the distance, RoboGames uses a 3-judge panel where each judge independently scores Aggression on a 0-5 point scale and Damage on a 0-6 point scale, for 11 points per judge and 33 points total across the panel. Aggression scoring examples given in the rules: a 5-0 split means one robot never attacked at all, a 4-1 split reflects significant one-sided dominance, and a 3-2 split covers matches where both robots attacked consistently (or, conversely, where both avoided each other about equally) — with credit for aggression specifically requiring 'translational movement toward the opponent,' not just spinning a weapon in place. Damage is bucketed into six severity tiers (trivial, cosmetic, minor, significant, major, massive) before being converted to a judge's point total. Pinning an opponent is capped at 15 seconds before the pinning robot must back off enough to let the opponent attempt to escape.

chunks.title: BattleBots: The TV-Scale Heavyweight Standard
chunks.body_md:
BattleBots is the most visible combat robotics competition to the general public, run as a televised series with a single professional-tier weight class: 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, with an allowance up to 500 lb for a robot that qualifies as a true walker using articulated legs and meets additional design criteria BattleBots specifies. This mirrors the same 100%-bonus-for-true-walkers pattern used across essentially every other ruleset in the sport, just at a far larger absolute mass than hobby classes.

One distinctive BattleBots requirement is a functional test for lifting/grappling weapons: any robot entering with a lifter, flipper, or grappling weapon must demonstrate, as part of pre-event inspection, that the weapon can actually lift 250 lb to a height of 12 inches. This is a meaningful bar — it means a flipper can't just look impressive on paper or in CAD, it has to prove it can flip a full-weight opponent in a live functional test before being cleared to compete, which keeps underpowered 'flippers' from entering the arena only to fail on air.

Every robot goes through BattleBots' full in-person technical and safety inspection, commonly referred to as 'the box,' before being cleared to fight — a far more rigorous process than most hobby-scale events can afford to run, reflecting both the higher stakes (250 lb robots at full power are genuinely dangerous) and BattleBots' larger operating budget and professional crew.

When a match runs the full duration without a knockout, BattleBots' published Judges' Guide (recent seasons) uses an 11-point scale per judge across a 3-judge panel: 5 points for Damage, 3 points for Aggression, and 3 points for Control. Damage is scored on the relative amount of non-cosmetic damage dealt to each robot — including self-inflicted damage and any system that stops working correctly by the end of the match, whether or not it looks visually dramatic. Aggression is scored on the frequency, severity, boldness, and intent of attacks a robot deliberately initiates against its opponent, rewarding a robot that presses the fight rather than one that merely survives. Control is scored on how well and how long a robot dictates the terms of the fight — pushing the opponent around, lifting it, pinning it, or using arena hazards/walls against it. This point split is not permanent: ahead of the BattleBots Pro League in 2026, the judging system was revised to merge Aggression with a new 'Engagement' concept into a single 5-point scored category, so competitors and analysts should always check the current season's official Judges' Guide rather than assume any one year's exact split carries forward. What has stayed constant across seasons is the baseline mechanical requirement: 250 lb standard weight, 500 lb walker allowance, and the mandatory 250 lb-to-12-inch lift test for any lifting/grappling weapon system.

chunks.title: Antweight World Series (AWS): The UK's Antweight-Scale Standard
chunks.body_md:
The Antweight World Series (AWS), administered in association with Bristol Bot Builders, is the primary UK/European ruleset for antweight-scale combat robotics, and it is built around a materially different, much lighter class ladder than the US SPARC standard: Antweight at 150 g (roller) / 225 g (non-roller), Fleaweight at 75 g / 113 g, and Nanoweight at 25 g / 38 g. There is no US equivalent to Fleaweight or Nanoweight at all — the US ladder's lightest class (1 lb antweight, or SPARC's own separately-named Fairyweight at 150 g) doesn't go nearly as small.

AWS's radio rules reflect the UK scene's longer history with analog and early digital RC systems: it explicitly permits 27 MHz, 40 MHz, 418 MHz, 433-434 MHz, 868 MHz, and 2.45 GHz, a wider allowed-frequency list than most modern 2.4GHz-only US rulesets, likely preserving compatibility with older UK-legal surface radio-control gear still in circulation at hobbyist level. Battery rules cap voltage at 24V and explicitly prohibit any battery containing liquid acid or free electrolyte (ruling out traditional wet-cell chemistries entirely, though this is largely moot in an era of LiPo/LiFe dominance).

Weapon safety rules under AWS are detailed: weapons must be remotely deactivable, any pressurized system (CO2, pneumatics) is capped at 100 psi (7 bar), and any detachable weapon component must remain tethered to the robot with a maximum tether length of 3 feet (914 mm) to prevent it becoming an uncontrolled projectile. The banned-weapons list closely tracks what other rulesets prohibit but is phrased slightly differently: glue or sticky-pad weapons, fluid-based weapons, string/entanglement weapons, flame-based weapons, using electricity itself as a weapon (e.g. deliberately shocking an opponent), explosive weapons, rotating weapons judged prone to shattering (a specific concern given how small and fast antweight-scale spinners can spin), and magnetic/inductive systems intended to interfere with an opponent.

Match structure: 3-minute maximum matches, a 10-second immobility countdown that ends a fight if one robot shows no controlled movement, a 20-second cap on pinning before release is required, and an automatic loss for any robot that touches the bottom of an arena pit. Clusterbots that mix roller and non-roller sub-units use an explicit formula — Roller weight allowance = Roller class limit − (2/3 × total non-roller weight) — to fairly balance the roller/non-roller weight bonus across a multi-unit entry rather than letting teams stack cheap non-roller mass to inflate their effective roller allowance.

chunks.title: Banned Weapons and Materials: What Every Major Org Agrees On
chunks.body_md:
Despite differences in wording, weight classes, and judging systems, the major combat robotics rulesets (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots, AWS/UK) converge on nearly the same core list of banned weapons and materials, because the underlying safety reasoning is identical everywhere: nothing that endangers spectators/officials beyond the arena barrier, nothing that permanently contaminates the arena surface for the next match, and nothing that makes damage impossible for judges/audiences to verify.

**Liquids and fluids**: banned almost everywhere, though NHRL's wording shows the two narrow exceptions most rulesets implicitly share: liquid expelled from the robot is banned generally, but liquid used purely as a fuel source is allowed, and liquid that turns gaseous shortly after leaving the robot (or before hitting the opponent) is also allowed — i.e. the ban targets a lasting liquid mess or a liquid weapon effect, not incidental fuel or something that evaporates before it can contaminate anything. AWS specifically calls out both 'fluid-based weapons' and separately bans batteries containing liquid acid or electrolyte.

**Untethered and over-speed projectiles**: NHRL puts a hard number on this where many rulesets only say 'no projectiles' — any projectile weapon is capped at 150 mph, and even a tethered projectile must not be designed in a way likely to become entangled with the opponent (blurring into the separate entanglement ban). NHRL defines entanglement itself precisely as any component 'designed to be entangled in the rotational or moving parts of the opponent,' a definition broad enough to cover string, tape, nets, or a deliberately snagging weapon geometry.

**Fire and flame**: banned by default everywhere, though a few large, heavily-supervised events (RoboGames, historically some BattleBots-adjacent exhibitions) allow specially pre-approved, licensed flamethrower weapons under strict extra safety conditions — this is very much the exception, not the rule, and never available at the antweight/beetleweight club level.

**Entanglement**: nets, string, tape, or any device meant to tangle an opponent's weapon or drivetrain is banned nearly everywhere (SPARC, RoboGames, AWS) because it can permanently disable a robot in a way that isn't 'damage' judges can score, and can be dangerous to retrieve after a match. A notable named exception: Germany's RoboGames-adjacent scene has historically permitted entanglement in a separate, clearly-labeled 'net-fighting' side bracket rather than mainstream weight-class combat.

**RF jamming / EMP / electrical weapons**: banned everywhere, since deliberately interfering with an opponent's radio control (rather than beating it in a fair fight) also risks jamming other robots' or the arena's own radio-linked safety systems — an inherently unacceptable risk at any event running multiple simultaneous transmitters.

**Untethered projectiles**: banned nearly universally (RoboGames explicitly, AWS via its tethered-weapon rule, SPARC generally) because anything that can leave the robot uncontrolled is an immediate spectator-safety hazard; where a detachable weapon component is allowed at all, it must remain tethered (AWS: 3 ft / 914 mm max).

**Explosives and hazardous materials**: universally banned, including flammable solids, and most rulesets also prohibit powders, sand, ball bearings, foams, and liquefied gases specifically because of arena-surface contamination risk (explicit in RoboGames' rules) rather than direct combat danger alone.

**Materials at the plastic-class level**: this is a narrower, class-specific restriction rather than a safety ban — plastic antweight/beetleweight forbid TPU, nylon, and fiber-reinforced composite filaments, not because they're dangerous, but to preserve the class's low-cost, low-damage design intent.

A builder moving between organizations should still read each event's current rulebook in full, since specific wording, exceptions (like Germany's net-fighting bracket), and edge cases (what counts as an 'approved' flamethrower, or exactly which magnetic effects are banned) do vary, but the underlying philosophy — no liquids, no uncontrolled fire, no entanglement, no jamming, no loose projectiles, no explosives — is close to universal across every major hobby ruleset in this research.

chunks.title: Core Safety Systems: Power Switches, Weapon Locks, and Radio Fail-Safes
chunks.body_md:
Three safety systems appear on essentially every rulebook's inspection checklist regardless of weight class or organization, because they address the three most common ways a combat robot can hurt someone outside the arena: an accidentally-live robot, an accidentally-spinning weapon during handling, and a robot that keeps moving after its driver loses control.

**Main power disconnect / removable link**: every ruleset requires a way to fully cut power to the robot's motors and weapon that doesn't require tools and can be operated quickly by the builder or a marshal. RoboGames is explicit about timing: the disconnect must be operable within 15 seconds without endangering the operator, and full deactivation of the robot must be achievable within 60 seconds. AWS (UK) simply requires it be 'externally accessible' and operable 'without tools.' Larger classes often add a secondary, more certain isolation method — a physically removable link or jumper that a marshal can pull even if a switch has failed or is hard to reach — on top of the primary switch, precisely because a bigger, more dangerous robot deserves more than one way to guarantee it goes dead.

**Weapon lock**: any robot with a weapon capable of moving under its own power (a spinning disc/drum, a lifting arm, a hammer) must have a physical lock fitted whenever it is powered on outside the arena — during transport, pit setup, and staging before a match. RoboGames requires this lock to be a clearly visible, high-visibility color (neon orange or similar) specifically so an inspector or bystander can tell at a glance whether a weapon is safed or live; NHRL requires a lock that prevents a spinning weapon from moving 'outside of the cage,' i.e. it must contain the weapon even if it somehow spins up unexpectedly. Locks are fitted before power-on and removed only once the robot is placed in the arena and the match is about to begin.

**Radio fail-safe**: the receiver/ESC system must be programmed so that losing the transmitter signal (turned off, out of range, battery dies, interference) causes all motion — drive and weapon alike — to stop immediately, rather than continuing at whatever the last received command was (which could mean a weapon left spinning at full speed or a drivetrain left driving into a wall or an official). This is tested directly at inspection: an inspector or the driver deliberately powers off or unplugs the transmitter while the robot is live, and watches to confirm the robot goes fully inert. NHRL calls this out as a mandatory pass/fail test every robot must clear before competing; AWS requires the same behavior ('robot shall cease all motion when the controlling transmitter is switched off') as a hard rule.

Together these three systems form the backbone of virtually every technical inspection checklist in the sport: an inspector will check for a functioning, accessible power disconnect, a properly colored and fitted weapon lock, and a passing fail-safe test, typically in that order, before moving on to weight, dimensions, and weapon-specific checks.

chunks.title: LiPo Battery Handling, Charging, and Arena Requirements
chunks.body_md:
Lithium-polymer (LiPo) batteries are the dominant power source across nearly every combat robot weight class, from plastic antweight up through TV-scale heavyweights, because of their excellent power-to-weight ratio — but that same energy density makes them the single most common fire-safety concern at any event, and pit safety rules around LiPo handling are taken very seriously after real incidents, including LiPo fires in the pit area at RoboGames 2017 that led directly to fireproof battery bags becoming mandatory rather than optional at many events afterward.

The near-universal practices that show up across event safety documents are: charge only inside a fireproof LiPo charging bag or a vented metal/ammo-can-style box, never inside a plastic tote, cardboard box, or bare on a table; never leave a battery charging unattended, even briefly — an unattended charging LiPo is treated as a serious pit-safety violation that can get a competitor removed from the event; inspect every battery before use for physical damage (punctures, cuts to the outer wrap, bent or corroded connectors) and especially for swelling/puffing, which indicates internal damage and means the cell should be retired immediately rather than risked in a fight; and never allow a battery to be crushed, punctured, or have its leads crossed/shorted, since any of these can trigger thermal runaway — the battery catching fire or venting violently.

Beyond individual battery handling, arena and venue-level requirements exist specifically because of LiPo risk: venues are commonly expected to be ventilated for roughly one full air exchange every 60 seconds, and any area where LiPo batteries are present (pits, charging stations, staging areas) should have a clear, obstruction-free evacuation route to open air, since a LiPo fire can produce toxic smoke quickly. AWS's rules add an antweight-specific voltage cap of 24V, and require that batteries not contain liquid acid or free electrolyte — ruling out old-style wet-cell chemistries entirely, though this is now largely a non-issue given LiPo and LiFe's dominance at every scale from fairyweight up.

For an antweight or plastic-antweight builder specifically, the practical rules of thumb that follow directly from event safety requirements are: buy a small fireproof LiPo bag (they are inexpensive and reusable across a builder's entire career), always charge in that bag on a non-flammable surface away from anything combustible, never charge overnight or walk away mid-charge, retire any cell that develops even mild puffing rather than trying to "get one more fight" out of it, and store spare batteries at storage voltage (roughly 3.8V/cell) rather than full charge when not competing soon, since long-term storage at full charge accelerates degradation and swelling risk.

chunks.title: Match Length, Win Conditions, and Judging Criteria
chunks.body_md:
Match structure is one of the more standardized parts of combat robotics rules across organizations: nearly every event, from UK antweight club nights to NHRL and BattleBots, runs 3-minute matches as the default duration, with the winner decided by one of a small set of standard outcomes rather than a running score kept throughout the fight.

**Win conditions, in rough order of how often they end a match**:
1. **Knockout (KO) / immobility**: a robot that shows no controlled, purposeful movement for a set count (commonly 10 seconds, as under AWS) is ruled out. Some rulesets apply this as a strict referee-operated countdown clock; others leave it to referee judgment of what counts as 'controlled movement' (e.g. a weapon still spinning uselessly on a robot that can no longer drive may or may not count as 'movement' depending on the event).
2. **Tap-out**: a driver can voluntarily concede to stop a match early, most often used when a robot is clearly beaten and continuing risks unnecessary damage or a safety issue (a stuck weapon, smoke, exposed wiring).
3. **Pit fall / arena hazard**: at venues with a pit or built-in hazard, touching the bottom of the pit is treated as an automatic loss under UK/AWS-style rules; most US hobby-class arenas are flat boxes without hazards, so this mainly applies to specific event designs.
4. **Judges' decision**: if the full match time elapses with both robots still mobile and neither has tapped out, a panel (commonly 3 judges) decides the winner. RoboGames formalizes this most explicitly: each judge scores Aggression (0-5 points) and Damage (0-6 points) independently, for 11 points per judge and 33 total across the panel. Damage is typically bucketed into severity tiers (trivial, cosmetic, minor, significant, major, massive) before being converted into points, and aggression specifically credits 'translational movement toward the opponent' rather than just activity in place. Other organizations (BattleBots, NHRL) also judge on a mix of damage, aggression, and control, but publish less granular public point breakdowns than RoboGames.

**Pinning and cornering limits**: to prevent a robot from winning simply by holding an opponent against a wall or under itself without actively fighting, most rulesets cap how long a pin can be held — 15 seconds under RoboGames, 20 seconds under AWS — after which the pinning robot must back off enough to give the opponent a real chance to escape or continue fighting; cornering an opponent against the arena wall is generally treated the same as a physical pin for this purpose.

**Between-match logistics**: some organizations also specify minimum time between a team's matches (RoboGames references a 40-minute minimum gap) to give builders enough time for repairs, battery swaps, and re-inspection before their next fight — a detail that matters a lot for a plastic antweight builder who may need to reprint or hot-glue a cracked chassis between rounds.

chunks.title: What a Technical/Safety Inspector Actually Checks
chunks.body_md:
Every combat robot, from a $30 plastic antweight to a $50,000 BattleBots heavyweight, passes through a technical and safety inspection before it is allowed to compete, and while the depth of inspection scales enormously with weight class, the checklist items are drawn from the same underlying list everywhere. For an antweight or plastic-antweight builder showing up to their first event, a realistic run-through of what an inspector checks looks roughly like this, in a typical order:

1. **Weigh-in**: the robot, fully assembled and ready to fight (batteries installed, all fasteners tight, nothing missing), is placed on a scale and must be at or under the class limit (e.g. 454 g for US antweight, 150 g for UK antweight/fairyweight, or the appropriate walker-bonus weight if claiming that allowance). Many inspectors also re-verify weight after any mid-event repair.
2. **Dimension/footprint check**: some rulesets (notably AWS/UK) also require the robot fit within a defined footprint (150mm x 150mm square for UK antweight-scale classes) with no overhang at any height, checked with a simple frame or template.
3. **Power disconnect check**: the inspector locates and tests the main power switch or removable link, confirming it is externally accessible, operable without tools, and actually cuts all power when used.
4. **Weapon lock check**: for any robot with an active weapon, the inspector confirms a proper high-visibility lock is fitted and prevents the weapon from moving while power is on, and that it's easy for pit staff to see at a glance whether the robot is 'safe' or 'live.'
5. **Radio fail-safe test**: the inspector or driver arms the robot, then deliberately turns off or unplugs the transmitter while watching the robot; a pass means all motion (drive and weapon) stops immediately, and repeats may be requested to rule out a fluke.
6. **Battery/wiring check**: batteries are inspected for physical damage, swelling, or exposed wiring; connectors are checked for secure fit and correct polarity; any battery pack that looks damaged or that exceeds the class's voltage cap (e.g. AWS's 24V limit) is rejected outright.
7. **Banned materials/weapons check**: the inspector visually confirms no banned weapon types are present (entanglement devices, liquid reservoirs, explosive/flame elements, RF-jamming hardware) and, for plastic-class entries, may spot-check that structural parts are visibly plastic and not a banned filament like TPU, nylon, or a carbon-fiber composite passed off as standard PLA/ABS.
8. **Sharp edge / pinch point check**: at even the smallest scale, inspectors look for exposed sharp edges, unshielded gears, or pinch points that could injure a handler during ordinary pit handling, independent of the robot's in-arena weapon.
9. **Sign-off**: once everything passes, the robot is tagged/logged as cleared to fight, sometimes with a sticker or wristband system tying the robot to its driver and confirmed weight class.

For a plastic antweight in particular, inspection is usually fast (often under two minutes) precisely because the class's material and weight limits are tight, weapon energy is low, and there's little to check beyond the basics above — one more reason it remains the easiest class to show up to an event with for the first time and get through check-in without surprises.

chunks.title: European and Other International Ruleset Variants
chunks.body_md:
Outside the US (SPARC/NHRL/RoboGames/BattleBots) and UK (AWS) rulesets, several other regional variants exist, generally built on the same underlying safety philosophy but with local adjustments for weight classes, allowed weapon types, or historical quirks.

**Fighting Robots Association (FRA)**, based in the UK, publishes its own build rules that are referenced across a number of UK and continental European events, generally complementing AWS's antweight-specific rules with guidance for a broader span of weight classes. FRA-affiliated documentation also circulates through European hobbyist mirrors (for example, a French robot-combat community site hosting an FRA build-rules PDF), reflecting how UK-style rules have propagated into continental European club scenes that don't have their own from-scratch rulebook.

**Germany** has historically taken a notably different approach to one specific banned-weapon category: rather than banning entanglement weapons outright the way SPARC, RoboGames, and AWS do, German events (associated with RoboGames-adjacent competition) have permitted entanglement devices (nets, tangling weapons) in a separate, clearly labeled 'net-fighting' side bracket kept apart from mainstream weight-class combat. This is the most commonly cited example of a national/regional ruleset carving out an explicit exception to an otherwise near-universal ban, rather than simply having laxer rules across the board.

**Australia**, via the RoboWars Australia community, is a useful counter-example to the assumption that 'international rules always mean lighter weight classes': it explicitly follows the SPARC ruleset and the same heavier US-style ladder rather than the UK/AWS scale — Australian Antweight is 1 lb (454 g), the same as US antweight, not the UK's 150 g class. Australia's ladder mirrors SPARC almost exactly (Antweight 1lb, Beetleweight 3lb, Mantisweight 6lb, Hobbyweight 12lb, Featherweight 30lb, Lightweight 60lb, Middleweight 120lb, Heavyweight 220lb) but adds one class the mainstream US ladder doesn't commonly run: a 340 lb (154 kg) Super Heavyweight tier above heavyweight. Non-wheeled robots get the standard 100% weight bonus at most classes, but that bonus shrinks to 35% specifically at the 340 lb Super Heavyweight level — presumably because a fully doubled 680 lb walking robot at that scale would be both impractical and disproportionately dangerous relative to the rest of the ladder. Australia also runs a distinct 'UltiBot' division for outdoor-terrain combat robots (30 kg for a mobile entrant, 25 kg for a fixed/stationary entrant), which has no equivalent in indoor-arena US/UK rules at all.

The overall pattern across international variants is consistency in the safety fundamentals (power disconnects, weapon locks, radio fail-safes, bans on liquids/explosives/jamming) with the most visible differences showing up in weight-class numbers and structure: the UK/AWS runs a much lighter, antweight-scale-and-below ladder (150 g down to 25 g) with a 50% non-roller bonus, while the US (SPARC/NHRL/RoboGames) and Australia (RoboWars) share a heavier ladder starting at 1 lb with a 100% walker bonus, and Australia extends that ladder one tier further with a 340 lb Super Heavyweight class at a reduced 35% bonus. Germany's net-fighting exception (permitting entanglement in a dedicated side bracket rather than mainstream classes) is the clearest example of a deliberate weapon-rule carve-out rather than a structural weight-class difference. A builder planning to compete internationally, or sourcing rules information from a non-domestic source, should treat both the weight-class numbers and the walker-bonus percentage as likely points of divergence, and should never assume a class name (especially 'Antweight') transfers its exact weight across borders without checking the specific ruleset.

chunks.title: Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast: The US Regional Event Circuit
chunks.body_md:
Beyond the handful of large, well-documented US organizations (NHRL, RoboGames, BattleBots), a wider circuit of regional, independently-run, SPARC-compliant events forms the backbone of where most antweight and plastic-antweight builders actually get their fight experience. Three names that come up repeatedly in the US hobby scene are Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast.

**Motorama** is one of the longest-running events on the US calendar, historically associated with Pennsylvania and more recently held in the Doswell, Virginia area, and is often treated as an early-season fixture that many builders use to debut a new antweight or plastic-antweight design before the rest of the year's events. Like most regional US events, it runs SPARC-compliant weight classes rather than maintaining its own separate rulebook, which is precisely the point of SPARC's existence: a robot built to spec for Motorama should need no changes to also compete at Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast, or a RoboGames combat bracket.

**Robot Ruckus** is a confirmed annual SPARC-compliant event co-located with Maker Faire Orlando at the Central Florida Fairgrounds (4603 W Colonial Dr, Orlando, FL). It splits its tournament format by class size: the insect classes (fairyweight, antweight, plastic-antweight, beetleweight) run double-elimination brackets, while the larger 12lb, 30lb, and 30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss-style fight format instead, reflecting how many more matches a small, cheap-to-repair antweight can realistically fight in a single day compared to a larger, slower-to-repair robot.

**Bot Blast** is a confirmed annual insectweight-focused event running a modified version of SPARC rather than stock SPARC. Its documented deviations are: a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots (unlike RoboGames, which runs a dedicated autonomous division), an immediate knockout — at the presiding official's discretion — for any robot found with an exposed or damaged LiPo battery during a match (a notable safety escalation beyond baseline SPARC, reflecting how seriously the hobby treats LiPo fire risk), and simplified judging criteria relative to full SPARC judging guidelines. Bot Blast explicitly discourages 'rules-lawyering' loopholes that give an unsportsmanlike advantage, a philosophy stated directly in its published rules.

Both events, along with Motorama, illustrate why SPARC's existence matters in practice: a plastic antweight or antweight built once to SPARC spec can travel between Motorama, Robot Ruckus, and Bot Blast (and on to RoboGames or a regional NHRL-adjacent event) with at most minor, clearly-documented local adjustments (like Bot Blast's exposed-LiPo rule) rather than a full rebuild for each event's own from-scratch rulebook.
